papers.title: The ever-expanding universe of botulinum neurotoxin in movement disorders.
papers.abstract: Botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) has become a cornerstone in the management of movement disorders since its introduction into neurological practice. Initially established as a first-line therapy for focal dystonias and other hyperkinetic conditions, its efficacy is supported by robust clinical evidence and guideline recommendations. BoNT exerts its therapeutic effects through inhibition of acetylcholine release via cleavage of SNARE proteins, resulting in reversible chemodenervation, with additional evidence supporting modulation of sensory pathways and central motor circuits. This present review intends to summarize the clinical use of BoNT beyond established ones in dystonia and spasticity, as expanding applications accrue. The expanse includes treatment of Parkinson and Non-Parkinson-related movement disorders, hyperexcitability syndromes, autonomic blockade and pain reduction. Emerging utility of BoNT clinical use include the applications at Intensive Care Unit, the pre-emptive use of BoNT during surgeries and the device aided BoNT deliveries. These developments highlight its evolving role as a versatile therapy beyond purely motor control. Despite growing clinical experience, many emerging indications remain supported by limited or heterogeneous evidence. Further studies are needed to define optimal patient selection, dosing strategies, and long-term outcomes. As understanding of disease mechanisms continues to evolve, BoNT is poised to remain at the forefront of personalized and precision-based therapies in movement disorders.

papers.title: An acoustic-only multivariable diagnostic model for Parkinson's disease using bowel sound acoustic signatures.
papers.abstract: BackgroundEarly detection of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains challenging due to the lack of reliable prodromal biomarkers. Non-invasive markers of gastrointestinal dysfunction are lacking.ObjectivesTo characterize bowel sound acoustic phenotypes in PD and evaluate their potential as non-invasive diagnostic markers by developing an acoustic-based predictive model.MethodsStandardized 5-min bowel sound recordings were collected from 120 PD patients and 100 controls. Thirteen acoustic features were extracted. LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) selected predictors for logistic regression models, internally validated with 1000 bootstrap resamples. The acoustic-only model was evaluated without refitting within the development cohort in 48 patients with Hoehn-Yahr stages 1-2 and 100 controls.ResultsPD patients exhibited fragmented, low-energy bowel sound patterns compared with controls. Acoustic features did not differ significantly by constipation status, while two duration measures differed by Hoehn-Yahr stage. A full-feature model incorporating acoustic and biochemical markers achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.8659. The acoustic-only model containing six predictors, three of which were statistically significant, yielded an AUC of 0.7999 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.737-0.852). Optimism-corrected AUCs were 0.839 and 0.784, respectively. In the early-stage subgroup, the AUC was 0.728 (95% CI, 0.644-0.806), with 68.75% sensitivity and 66.00% specificity at the fixed probability threshold of 0.50.ConclusionsPD patients exhibit distinct bowel sound acoustic phenotypes. Acoustic features provided discrimination between PD patients and controls, including in early-stage disease. This non-invasive profiling approach offers a promising functional biomarker candidate for multimodal PD assessment.

papers.title: Charting the future: A multi-setting medical chart study of advance care planning in Parkinson's disease and atypical Parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAdvance Care Planning (ACP) enables people with progressive diseases to document and communicate future treatment preferences. For Parkinson's disease (PD) and atypical parkinsonism (AP), ACP is particularly important because of disease complexity, symptom burden, the progressive nature of the disease, and cognitive decline, yet its implementation across care settings remains unclear.MethodsWe conducted a medical chart review of 189 deceased patients with PD or AP who died in nursing homes (n = 91), hospitals (n = 58), or at home (n = 40) in the Netherlands. For patients who died at home, data were obtained from their general practice records. Data on treatment preferences, care discussions and palliative care goals were extracted at one year and six weeks before death.ResultsDocumentation of treatment preferences increased towards death but differed markedly between settings. Nursing homes recorded resuscitation and ICU limitations early and comprehensively, whereas hospitals made major updates only in the final weeks of life. In general practices, ACP documentation was limited. Nursing homes and hospitals more frequently addressed disease-specific scenarios, palliative sedation and end-of-life issues, while general practices more often reported preferred place of death and euthanasia. Palliative care goals in nursing homes covered all domains, while in hospitals and general practices they mainly related to physical aspects.ConclusionACP remains inconsistently documented and frequently delayed until the final weeks of life, when crises or cognitive decline may hinder meaningful participation. Earlier, iterative ACP-supported by clinician training, PD-specific guidance, and system-level measures such as ACP prompts in electronic medical records-could foster a more proactive and person-centered palliative approach aligned with patient values throughout the disease trajectory.

papers.title: Perspectives on ionizing radiation and Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Emerging evidence from terrestrial cohorts suggests that ionizing radiation (IR) exposure may increase the risk of Parkinson's disease (PD). Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying IR-induced PD is therefore critical for assessing health risks, particularly in the context of long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. This perspective explores mechanistic pathways that may support causal links between IR and PD and highlights experimental and epidemiological approaches relevant for strengthening causal inference.

papers.title: Brain functional mechanisms of acupuncture treatment for early-stage non-tremor Parkinson's disease: a resting-state fMRI study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To observe the modulatory effects of acupuncture in early-stage non-tremor Parkinson's disease (PD) patients using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and to determine the correlation between its changes and clinical indicators. METHODS: This observational study included 35 patients with early Parkinson's disease who received multi-target acupuncture treatment combined with regular levodopa therapy (twice weekly for 12 weeks) in the traditional Chinese medicine department. They were classified as the observation group and the study period was from January 2023 to December 2024. The observation group received acupuncture and underwent rs-fMRI scanning at baseline and post-treatment. A healthy control group underwent a single rs-fMRI scan at baseline. Post-treatment imaging and clinical data from the observation group were compared with those of the healthy control group. Primary outcomes were changes in rs-fMRI-derived degree centrality (DC), functional connectivity (FC), and fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF). Secondary outcomes included clinical scale improvements and correlations between imaging metrics and clinical scores. RESULTS: After treatment, the observation group showed significant improvements in MDS-UPDRS-III, MoCA, 10MWT, TUG, and PDQ-39 scores (all p CONCLUSION: Acupuncture treatment was associated with improvements in motor function, walking speed, and cognition in early-stage non-tremor PD, with potential mechanisms involving downregulated precuneus DC/FC and enhanced local activity. Furthermore, the change in right precuneus DC, which correlated significantly with both motor and cognitive improvements, may serve as a potential neuroimaging biomarker for treatment-induced clinical recovery.

papers.title: Eyes-closed finger-tapping task for assessing visual dependence in temporal motor control in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Impaired motor automaticity in Parkinson's disease (PD) may increase reliance on visual feedback, but its role in stabilizing repetitive movements remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To quantify the effect of eye closure on finger tapping and identify performance features reflecting visual dependence in PD. METHODS: Forty-five individuals with PD (74.0 ± 6.6 years; 21 women) and 20 age-matched healthy controls (HC; 74.6 ± 5.5 years; 13 women) performed 10-s index finger-to-thumb tapping under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. A wearable device recorded metacarpophalangeal flexion-extension angles at 1 kHz, with 30-Hz low-pass filtering. Six metrics were computed: the mean and variability of amplitude, velocity, and inter-peak interval. Eye-closure effects were estimated as r = ln(closed/open) and analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model with group, side, age, and sex as fixed effects and subject as a random intercept. RESULTS: A nominal group effect was observed only for interval variability (p CONCLUSION: The opposing numerical changes in tapping-interval variability in the PD and HC groups raise the possibility that visual input may contribute differently to temporal stability during repetitive movements in the two groups, warranting further investigation.

papers.title: Modulators selectively reshape α-synuclein phase transitions.
papers.abstract: Protein phase transitions govern numerous diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders. In Parkinson's disease, distinct species of the protein α-synuclein undergo phase transitions from disordered to ordered β-rich states. The emerging species and transitions between them can be reshaped by modulators, e.g., small molecules, peptides or antibodies. Here, we use coarse-grained simulations to understand the effect of modulators on the thermodynamics and kinetics of α-synuclein phase transitions. Each protein is represented as a morphing particle that transforms from a soft sphere (disordered) to a hard spherocylinder (β-rich). Modulators are modeled as soft isotropic particles mimicking peptides. Purely repulsive modulators do not alter the final outcome; that is, fibrils form following the same mechanisms independently of the modulator concentration. Attractive interactions toward the disordered protein dose-dependently slow down fibrillization by stabilizing intermediate species, including persistent disordered heteroclusters. Specific attraction to the β-rich state shortens fibrils through direct modulator surface "capping" that introduces kinetic barriers to monomer templating at the fibril ends and inhibits fibril elongation. Overall, these results link modulator properties and environmental conditions to nucleation, fibril elongation, and off-pathway trapping, providing a quantitative roadmap for designing interventions that redirect phase transitions toward desirable endpoints.

papers.title: Clemastine alleviates Parkinson's disease pathology by activating the AMPK/mTOR pathway and enhancing autophagic flux.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a debilitating neurodegenerative disorder with no available cure, underscoring the urgent need for novel therapeutics. This study employed the comprehensive bioinformatic analyses and the experimental models to investigate the potential of clemastine (CLE) for PD treatment. Bioinformatics identified 12 distinct cell subtypes and 577 differentially expressed genes in dopaminergic neurons (DaNs), along with 167 potential PD-relevant CLE targets. papers.title: Targeting Nrf2 Signaling in Parkinson's Disease: Mechanisms, Strategies, and Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons and the accumulation of α-synuclein. Disease progression is driven by a complex interplay of chronic oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. As a central regulator of the cellular antioxidant response, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) protects against these cellular insults by driving the expression of various cytoprotective genes. In this review, we summarize the regulatory mechanisms of the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway and evaluate how its activation counteracts core PD pathologies. We also highlight the extensive crosstalk between Nrf2 and other major signaling networks that collectively determine dopaminergic neuronal survival. Finally, we examine the therapeutic potential of current Nrf2 modulators, including natural phytochemicals, clinical-stage candidates, and repurposed drugs, and critically discuss the pharmacokinetic barriers, electrophilic off-target toxicities, and the Nrf2 paradox that must be overcome to successfully translate these compounds into disease-modifying therapies for PD, highlighting the transition toward non-covalent PPI inhibitors.

papers.title: Effect of freeze-thaw cycle induced oligomers on alpha-synuclein liquid-liquid phase separation and aggregation.
papers.abstract: Protein aggregation in the form of amyloid fibrils is linked with the onset and progression of several widespread and incurable disorders, including neurodegenerative Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Despite decades of research and countless attempts to discover potential aggregation-altering treatment modalities, there are still no effective cures for the majority of amyloid-related disorders. This is, in part, due to our incomplete understanding of the underlying factors that influence the phase separation and aggregation of these various disease-related proteins. Over the last few years, it has been shown that even factors such as storage conditions or sample preincubation times can affect the formation kinetics of amyloid fibrils. In the case of alpha-synuclein, even the protein purification procedure yielded different concentrations of oligomeric species, which altered the aggregation mechanism. In this work, we further explore the role of alpha-synuclein oligomers by inducing their formation via freeze-thaw cycles and analyzing their effect on liquid-liquid and liquid-solid phase transitions. Using real-time kinetic monitoring, brightfield microscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and atomic force microscopy, we show that the presence of freeze-thaw cycle induced alpha-synuclein oligomers has significant effects on its condensate assembly and subsequent aggregation, as well as the final structure of the formed aggregates.

papers.abstract: Current non-invasive assessments for Parkinson's disease (PD) are predominantly single-modality, leaving an unmet need for an integrated platform combining biomolecular and biomechanical detection. Here, an integrated dual-mode sensing platform based on a flexible non-woven fabric (NWFs) device for PD is provided. Silver nano-contacts are electrolessly deposited onto cotton fibers to form a biomimetic spider-leg-like microarchitecture, which concurrently supports localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) for surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) and strain-responsive piezoresistive behavior. papers.title: Mesenchymal stromal cells in age-related neurodegenerative disorders: mechanisms, translational barriers, and precision strategies.
papers.abstract: Ageing remodels the neuroimmune, metabolic, and vascular environment in ways that accelerate neuronal vulnerability and constrain tissue repair. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) and MSC-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs) are therefore attractive candidates for neurodegenerative disorders because their effects extend beyond cell replacement to coordinated paracrine, immunomodulatory, trophic, and vascular regulation. This critical review evaluates the biological rationale, disease-specific evidence, translational limitations, and precision-development strategies for MSC-based interventions in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple system atrophy, and vascular dementia, whilst using selected rare hereditary neurodegenerative disorders as exploratory boundary cases. Current evidence supports three interconnected modes of action: reprogramming maladaptive neuroimmune responses; preserving neuronal homeostasis through trophic support, mitochondrial rescue, and proteostasis regulation; and restoring the neurovascular unit and blood-brain barrier. However, reproducible clinical efficacy remains limited by variation in tissue source, donor age, manufacturing, potency, dose, route, and outcome selection, as well as poor central nervous system exposure and inadequate patient stratification. Ageing-related changes in both the recipient microenvironment and the cellular product further complicate translation. Future development should replace empirical cell administration with mechanism-defined products, validated potency assays, quantitative biodistribution, biomarker-guided enrolment, engineered cells or vesicles, rational combinations, and trials using disease-modifying endpoints. papers.title: Association of Fecal Calprotectin with Motor and Nonmotor Features in Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease and Atypical Parkinsonism.
papers.journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Gut inflammation and microbiota dysregulation are increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD). Fecal calprotectin, a neutrophil-derived protein and marker of intestinal inflammation, may serve as a non-invasive indicator of gut-brain axis dysfunction in parkinsonian disorders. To evaluate fecal calprotectin levels in idiopathic Parkinson's disease (IPD) and atypical parkinsonian syndromes-progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and multiple system atrophy (MSA)-and examine their relationship with motor and non-motor features. METHODS: In this case-control study, 130 patients (IPD = 94, PSP = 23, MSA = 13) and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were enrolled. All participants underwent detailed clinical evaluation, including the movement disorder society-unified Parkinson's disease rating scale (MDS-UPDRS), Hoehn and Yahr staging, the non-motor symptoms scale (NMSS), the Rome IV criteria for constipation, and the Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA). Fecal calprotectin (μg/g stool) was quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and correlated with clinical parameters. RESULTS: Mean fecal calprotectin was significantly higher in IPD and PSP than in controls ( P < 0.01), whereas MSA showed no significant difference. Elevated fecal calprotectin correlated positively with total NMSS scores ( r ≈ 0.3, P < 0.05) and inversely with MoCA scores, indicating a greater non-motor symptom burden and poorer cognitive performance. No significant correlation was observed with MDS-UPDRS motor scores. Among the NMSS domains, sleep/fatigue, mood/apathy, perceptual problems, memory, and sexual domains exhibited the strongest associations. CONCLUSIONS: Fecal calprotectin is elevated in IPD and PSP and is more strongly associated with non-motor than motor manifestations. papers.title: Short-term Classification of Neurodegenerative Diseases using Time-series Features Based on Analysis of Gait Dynamics.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurodegenerative Diseases (NDDs) refer to disorders, leading to the gradual degeneration of neurons in the human nervous system and profoundly affecting individuals' motor and cognitive functions. Early diagnosis and monitoring of the progression of NDDs are of critical importance. OBJECTIVE: The primary aim of this study is to present an automatic diagnostic method using time-domain analysis of short-term gait signals of two consecutive steps, for the classification of Parkinson's Disease (PD), Huntington's Disease (HD), Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), and a Healthy Control Group (HC). MATERIAL AND METHODS: This analytical study used datasets from PhysioNet, including 64 five-minute recordings from 13 individuals with ALS, 15 with Parkinson's, 20 with Huntington's, and 16 healthy individuals. To reduce noise and enhance signal quality, a median filter was applied. The preprocessed gait signals were then systematically segmented into consecutive two-step windows, which were used to construct the feature vectors. Finally, the constructed feature vectors were used as inputs for both linear and nonlinear classifiers. The proposed method was evaluated by calculating the accuracy index. RESULTS: The quaternary classification of ALS vs. PD vs. HD vs. HC using the bag-tree classifier achieved an accuracy of 82.8%. Furthermore, for the binary classifications of HC vs. HD, HC vs. ALS, HC vs. PD and NDD vs. HC, the accuracies were 88.4%, 97.6%, 90% and 89.1%, respectively. CONCLUSION: Gait dynamics analysis has a high potential for the rapid diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases. Short term analysis in two consecutive stages enables the use of the Kinect sensor for gait analysis.

papers.title: The Mechanism of Dietary Intervention in Delaying Brain Aging and Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.abstract: With the global aging population, age-related neurodegenerative diseases and cerebrovascular diseases have become major public health challenges. As a modifiable lifestyle strategy, dietary intervention shows significant potential in delaying brain aging and reducing the risk of neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases. Caloric restriction (CR) and dietary restriction (DR), two important nutritional intervention approaches, exhibit substantial neuroprotective potential through multiple mechanisms. This review systematically summarizes the mechanisms of CR and DR in brain aging and related diseases, focusing on: (1) modulating gene expression and epigenetic modifications; (2) regulating proteostasis and autophagy; (3) inhibiting neuroinflammation to delay inflammaging; (4) improving mitochondrial function and oxidative homeostasis; and (5) optimizing nutrient-sensing pathways and metabolism. Additionally, this review discusses the mechanistic evidence of CR and DR in disease models such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Parkinson's Disease (PD), stroke, and Vascular Dementia (VaD). Despite promising preclinical findings, their clinical translation faces challenges including individual variability, safety concerns, and uncertainty regarding mechanism prioritization. Future research should focus on conducting more high-quality clinical trials, integrating multi-omics technologies with precision nutrition strategies to promote the practical application of CR and DR in advancing healthy brain aging.

papers.title: Gut oralisation signatures in Parkinson's disease: an integrative multi-study analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) compromises oral hygiene and oral health, potentially increasing oral bacterial input to the gut. Whether PD is associated with reproducible faecal enrichment of oral disease-linked taxa remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether oral disease-linked taxa are enriched in the faecal microbiota of individuals with PD. METHODS: We conducted a pooled re-analysis of 23 faecal 16S rRNA datasets, comprising 3,594 PD and control samples. eHOMD was used to resolve oral-associated taxa, including caries/endodontic- and periodontitis-linked taxa. SILVA-based profiles were used to assess community diversity and ordination patterns. Differential-abundance analyses accounted for variation between studies. RESULTS: PD samples showed heterogeneous but reproducible enrichment of oral disease-linked taxa, with a prominent caries/endodontic-associated component. The cariogenic-enriched subgroup showed reduced evenness and increased representation of oral taxa including Streptococcus mutans CONCLUSIONS: This pooled re-analysis identifies a gut oralization-associated signal in a subset of individuals with PD. Faecal enrichment of oral-associated taxa may represent one component of gut microbiome heterogeneity and may indirectly reflect variation in oral ecosystem status, supporting oral health assessment in future PD microbiome studies.

papers.title: Dietary heme iron intake and common hemochromatosis HFE polymorphisms have similar associations with brain MRI phenotypes: a UK Biobank cohort study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Brain iron accumulation is associated with aging and neurodegeneration, but how individual genetics and dietary iron intake affect brain iron is not well understood. Hemochromatosis is a genetic disorder arising from single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the HFE gene, causing iron overload and brain iron accumulation, and is associated with accelerated brain aging. OBJECTIVE: This cross-sectional study examined how dietary iron intake and hemochromatosis-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms are associated with brain MRI phenotypes sensitive to iron. METHODS: We used a subset of the UK Biobank (N=24,223 participants) to investigate associations between dietary heme and non-heme iron intake (dietary predictors), HFE SNPs rs1799945 and rs1800562 (genetic predictors), brain quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) and T2* MRI phenotypes (primary outcomes) using multiple regression. We also investigated associations of HFE SNPs and dietary intake with hemoglobin, anemia risk, and MRI-derived liver iron levels as markers of systemic iron status. We compared brain QSM for rs1799945 and rs1800562 homozygotes and rs1799945/rs1800562 compound heterozygotes relative to control genotype subjects without either HFE SNP using ANCOVA and Tukey-Kramer post-hoc testing. Significance was set at false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05. RESULTS: Intake of dietary heme iron and both HFE SNPs were associated with increased QSM and decreased T2* MRI intensities (FDR<0.05), a pattern associated with increased brain iron levels. Non-heme iron intake was associated with a slight, but statistically significant, decrease in QSM and increase in T2* intensity, which is consistent with less brain iron. Both SNPs and heme iron intake were associated with higher hemoglobin and MRI-derived liver iron levels. papers.title: Pharmacological Inhibition of Histamine N-Methyltransferase Markedly Improves Hypersomnia in a Mouse Model of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. In addition to motor symptoms, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) occurs frequently in patients with PD and severely impairs their quality of life. Current pharmacotherapies for EDS in PD are often associated with adverse effects. However, clinical studies have yielded inconsistent results, underscoring the need for safer, more effective treatment strategies. Histamine plays a pivotal role in maintaining wakefulness in the brain and is primarily inactivated by histamine N-methyltransferase (HNMT), the major enzyme responsible for histamine clearance in the central nervous system. We previously demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of HNMT markedly elevates brain histamine levels and potently promotes wakefulness in mouse models of narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia, suggesting that targeting HNMT may also be beneficial for treating hypersomnia in PD. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of HNMT ameliorates hypersomnia in a 6-hydroxydopamine-induced mouse model of PD. We first confirmed dopaminergic neuronal loss and hypersomnia during the active phase in a mouse model of PD. Pharmacological inhibition of HNMT with metoprine robustly increased wakefulness, markedly reduced NREM and REM sleep, and prolonged sleep latency. Metoprine also reduced sleep-wake bout fragmentation, indicating the sustained consolidation of wakefulness. In direct comparison, metoprine produced stronger and more sustained wake-promoting effects than other wake-promoting agents. These findings indicate that HNMT inhibition represents a promising and mechanistically distinct therapeutic approach for EDS in PD.

papers.title: Towards a Better Definition of Patient-Centered Therapeutic Strategy of Parkinson's Disease: An Opinion Paper.
papers.abstract: Recent Parkinson's disease (PD) treatment guidelines remain predominantly drug- and stage-centric and only inconsistently articulate a patient-centered medication strategy. We aimed to identify this gap and propose pragmatic, consensus-based principles for fully individualized, preference-sensitive pharmacological care across the patient journey. Seventeen movement disorder experts from eight European countries convened (March 2026) and generated key clinical questions spanning early to advanced PD. Panelists completed an anonymized questionnaire; semantic AI supported identification of areas of consensus and dissensus, followed by a single-round Delphi-style discussion to refine agreed statements. The panel reached consensus on eight statements across five focus areas: (i) incorporating patient characteristics and contextual factors underrepresented in guidelines (comorbidities, co-medications, behavioral/cognitive risk, non-motor symptom burden, and-when appropriate-genetics); (ii) treating therapy initiation as a longitudinal process with shared decision-making, education, and non-pharmacological foundations; (iii) legitimizing watchful waiting or dose reduction in selected scenarios; (iv) using both motor and non-motor symptoms and lifestyle goals as primary drivers of oral therapy selection; and (v) transparently managing evidence gaps while providing good-practice guidance on reassessment. Examples on how these recommendations can be used to plan a therapy strategy are presented for different patients' personae. In conclusion, a patient-centered medication strategy in PD should be explicit, structured, and revisited over time, aligning therapeutic choices with symptoms, risks, context, and individual goals and preferences. A wide range of treatments must always be available throughout the patient's care pathway to allow for greater individualization of care, particularly regarding treatment sequencing, drug combinations, and dosage thresholds. papers.title: Conformational allocation of mitofusin 2 in neuronal mitochondrial dynamics: Mechanisms and therapeutic targeting.
papers.abstract: Neurons must sustain functional mitochondria far from the cell body. Mitofusin 2 (MFN2), a dynamin-like large guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase), coordinates outer mitochondrial membrane remodeling with axonal transport, bioenergetic support, inter-organelle communication, and stress-responsive quality control. Studying these activities separately obscures how disruption of one protein produces diverse neuronal phenotypes. We propose a testable conformational-allocation framework in which molecular state distributions and transition kinetics bias MFN2 participation across cellular outputs. Integrating structural and functional evidence, we distinguish experimentally resolved mechanisms from working models. Variants associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) are compared by the molecular step or functional output affected. Fusion loss alone does not capture this mechanistic diversity. Structure-guided docking supports local compatibility at a shallow, conformationally conditional C-terminal surface, without establishing native accessibility, affinity, or therapeutic response. CMT2A provides the strongest context for intervention, combining causal genetics, direct mitofusin engagement studies, and multiscale rescue. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) provides secondary preclinical evidence, whereas Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases remain exploratory. The mitofusin pathway is chemically tractable, but paralog selectivity and state-dependent target engagement remain unresolved. A state- and variant-informed strategy may better match intervention to the affected output than indiscriminate enhancement of fusion.
